SECTIONS.label: Ch 1
SECTIONS.title: Units, dimensions, and estimation
ideas: SI base units for mechanics: meter (m), kilogram (kg), second (s). Everything else is built from them: newton $\text{N} = \text{kg·m/s}^2$, joule $\text{J} = \text{N·m}$, watt $\text{W} = \text{J/s}$, pascal $\text{Pa} = \text{N/m}^2$.

Convert units by multiplying by 1 written as a ratio: $72\ \text{km/h} \times \frac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}} \times \frac{1\ \text{h}}{3600\ \text{s}} = 20\ \text{m/s}$. Squared or cubed units convert twice or three times: $1\ \text{cm}^3 = (10^{-2}\ \text{m})^3 = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3$.
Dimensional analysis catches wrong equations: both sides must have the same dimensions, and you can only add quantities with the same units. Arguments of $\sin$, $\exp$, $\ln$ must be dimensionless.
Report answers to about three significant figures (the precision of the data), with units, and a sign or direction when the quantity is a vector.
Fermi estimates: round to powers of ten, multiply, and sanity-check the order of magnitude. Clicker questions love these.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 2
SECTIONS.title: Vectors: components and algebra
ideas: A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has only size. Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum are vectors. Distance, speed, mass, energy and time are scalars.

Components turn vector problems into two ordinary problems: $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ measured counterclockwise from the $+x$ axis. Going back: $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$ (check the quadrant from the signs of the components).
Add vectors by adding components: $\vec R = \vec A + \vec B \Rightarrow R_x = A_x + B_x,\ R_y = A_y + B_y$. Subtracting $\vec B$ means adding $-\vec B$ (flip both components).
Unit vectors $\hat i, \hat j, \hat k$ point along $x, y, z$: $\vec A = A_x\hat i + A_y\hat j$. Multiplying by a scalar scales the magnitude (negative scalar reverses direction).

Dot product $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x + A_yB_y$ (a scalar; used for work). Cross product $|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\theta$ (a vector perpendicular to both; used for torque and angular momentum; right-hand rule).

SECTIONS.label: Ch 3.1–3.4
SECTIONS.title: Motion in one dimension
ideas: Position $x(t)$, displacement $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$ (can be negative; distance cannot). Average velocity $\bar v = \Delta x/\Delta t$; instantaneous velocity $v = dx/dt$ (slope of the $x$–$t$ graph). Acceleration $a = dv/dt$ (slope of the $v$–$t$ graph).
Graphs: slope of $x$–$t$ is velocity; slope of $v$–$t$ is acceleration; area under $v$–$t$ is displacement; area under $a$–$t$ is change in velocity.
Constant acceleration gives four equations. Each one is missing one variable ($x$, $v$, $a$ or $t$); pick the equation that omits the quantity you neither know nor want.
Speeding up means $v$ and $a$ have the same sign; slowing down means opposite signs. Negative acceleration is not the same as slowing down.
With calculus: $v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a\,dt$, $x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t v\,dt$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 3.5–3.6
SECTIONS.title: Free fall
ideas: Near Earth's surface, ignoring air resistance, every object accelerates downward at $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ regardless of mass. Choose up as positive and use $a = -g$ throughout the flight, including at the top.

At the highest point the velocity is zero but the acceleration is still $-g$. The time up equals the time down for a launch-and-return to the same height, and the return speed equals the launch speed.
A dropped object: $v = -gt$, $y = y_0 - \tfrac12 gt^2$, impact speed $\sqrt{2gh}$. Thrown up at $v_0$: max height $v_0^2/(2g)$, time to top $v_0/g$.
When the landing height differs from the launch height, use $y = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac12 g t^2$ and solve the quadratic; keep the positive root.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 4.1–4.2
SECTIONS.title: Motion in two dimensions
ideas: Position, velocity and acceleration are vectors: $\vec r = x\hat i + y\hat j$, $\vec v = d\vec r/dt$, $\vec a = d\vec v/dt$. The $x$ and $y$ motions are independent: solve each with the 1D equations, linked only by time.

The velocity vector is tangent to the path. The acceleration vector points toward the inside of a curve; it has a component along the velocity (changing speed) and one perpendicular (changing direction).
Average velocity is displacement over time (a vector); average speed is distance over time (a scalar). On a round trip the average velocity is zero.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 4.3
SECTIONS.title: Projectile motion
ideas: A projectile has $a_x = 0$ (constant horizontal velocity) and $a_y = -g$ (free fall vertically). Launch components: $v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta$, $v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta$.
Time of flight comes from the vertical equation; horizontal range is then $x = v_{0x}t$. At the top $v_y = 0$ but $v_x$ is unchanged, so the speed at the top is $v_0\cos\theta$, not zero.
Level ground shortcuts: $T = 2v_0\sin\theta/g$, $R = v_0^2\sin(2\theta)/g$ (max at $45^\circ$; complementary angles give equal ranges), $H = v_0^2\sin^2\theta/(2g)$.
Horizontal launch from height $h$: $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$, $x = v_0 t$; impact speed $\sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}$ (energy works too).
The trajectory is a parabola: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g x^2}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 4.4–4.5
SECTIONS.title: Uniform circular motion and relative motion
ideas: Moving in a circle at constant speed still means accelerating, because the velocity's direction changes. The centripetal acceleration points toward the center with magnitude $a_c = v^2/r$.
Period $T$ is the time for one revolution: $v = 2\pi r/T$, so $a_c = 4\pi^2 r/T^2$. Angular speed $\omega = 2\pi/T$ and $v = r\omega$, $a_c = \omega^2 r$.
If the speed also changes there is a tangential acceleration $a_t = dv/dt$; the total acceleration is the vector sum of $a_c$ (radial) and $a_t$ (tangential).
Relative velocity: $\vec v_{A/C} = \vec v_{A/B} + \vec v_{B/C}$ (subscripts chain like fractions). A boat heading straight across a river is carried downstream; its ground velocity is the vector sum.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 5.1–5.5
SECTIONS.title: Newton’s laws of motion
ideas: First law: with zero net force an object keeps a constant velocity (including staying at rest). "At rest" and "moving at constant speed in a straight line" are the same situation dynamically.
Second law: $\sum\vec F = m\vec a$. Net force and acceleration point the same way. Apply it separately in $x$ and $y$: $\sum F_x = ma_x$, $\sum F_y = ma_y$.
Third law: forces come in pairs acting on different objects, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The pair of "Earth pulls on ball" is "ball pulls on Earth", never the normal force.
Mass measures inertia (kg) and is the same everywhere; weight $w = mg$ is a force (N) and depends on $g$.
Forces are interactions: every force on your object comes from something touching it (contact forces: normal, tension, friction, push) or from gravity (long range). Name the agent for each.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 5.6–5.7
SECTIONS.title: Common forces and free-body diagrams
ideas: Normal force $N$: perpendicular to the surface, as large as needed to prevent the object from sinking in. It is not always $mg$: on an incline $N = mg\cos\theta$; in an accelerating elevator $N = m(g + a)$; with an extra downward push it grows.
Tension $T$: along the rope, same magnitude at both ends of a massless rope, pulls (never pushes). An ideal pulley changes direction, not magnitude.
Weight $mg$ down; friction parallel to the surface, opposing sliding (or the tendency to slide); spring force $F = -kx$.

Free-body diagram recipe: isolate one object as a dot; draw every force on it with a label and agent; choose axes (along the acceleration is smartest, tilted for inclines); resolve; write $\sum F_x = ma_x$ and $\sum F_y = ma_y$.
Equilibrium means $\vec a = 0$: every component sum is zero. This is how you solve for tensions in hanging signs and cables.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 6.1
SECTIONS.title: Applying Newton’s laws
ideas: Multi-object systems (Atwood machines, blocks connected by ropes, stacked blocks): draw one free-body diagram per object, use the same $a$ magnitude for objects tied together, and add the equations to eliminate the tension.
Frictionless incline: $a = g\sin\theta$ down the slope, independent of mass. Add friction later as an extra term.
Elevator problems: the scale reads the normal force, $N = m(g + a)$ with $a$ positive upward. In free fall $N = 0$ ("weightless").
Blocks pushed together: treat the whole system to get $a = F/(m_1+m_2)$, then isolate one block to get the contact force $m_2 a$.
Sanity checks: heavier side of an Atwood machine accelerates down; $a$ must be less than $g$; tension must lie between the two weights.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 6.2
SECTIONS.title: Friction
ideas: Static friction adjusts itself to prevent sliding, up to a maximum $f_s \le \mu_s N$. It is an inequality; only at the verge of slipping is $f_s = \mu_s N$.
Kinetic friction has a fixed magnitude $f_k = \mu_k N$ while sliding, directed opposite the relative motion. Usually $\mu_k < \mu_s$.
Friction depends on the normal force, not on the weight directly and not on contact area. Increase $N$ (push down) and friction rises.
Incline: an object stays put if $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$; once sliding, $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.
Friction can point in the direction of motion (it is what accelerates a car forward, and what keeps a box from sliding off an accelerating truck bed).

SECTIONS.label: Ch 6.3–6.4
SECTIONS.title: Centripetal force, banked curves, and drag
ideas: "Centripetal force" is not a new force. It is the name for the net force component toward the center, $\sum F_{\text{radial}} = mv^2/r$, supplied by whatever real forces are present: tension, friction, normal force, gravity.
Flat curve: friction supplies it, so $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$. Banked curve with no friction: $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$.
Vertical circles: at the bottom $T - mg = mv^2/r$ (tension largest); at the top $T + mg = mv^2/r$, so the minimum speed to keep a taut string or stay on a loop is $v = \sqrt{gr}$.
Drag grows with speed ($F_D = \tfrac12 C\rho A v^2$ for air). Terminal speed is reached when drag equals weight: net force zero, constant velocity, $v_t = \sqrt{2mg/(C\rho A)}$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 12.1–12.2
SECTIONS.title: Static equilibrium and torque
ideas: Torque measures a force's ability to rotate an object about a pivot: $\tau = rF\sin\theta = F\,d_\perp$ (lever arm $d_\perp$ is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force). Counterclockwise is usually taken positive.
Static equilibrium needs both $\sum\vec F = 0$ and $\sum\tau = 0$ about any point. Choose the pivot where an unknown force acts so that it drops out of the torque equation.
Weight acts at the center of gravity. A uniform beam's weight acts at its midpoint.
Classic set-ups: seesaw/balance ($m_1d_1 = m_2d_2$), beam on two supports, ladder against a wall (friction at the floor, normal at the wall), hanging sign with a strut.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 14.1–14.4
SECTIONS.title: Static fluids
ideas: Density $\rho = m/V$ (water: $1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$). Pressure $P = F/A$ (Pa); atmospheric pressure $P_0 = 1.013\times10^5$ Pa.

Pressure increases with depth: $P = P_0 + \rho g h$. Gauge pressure is $\rho g h$ (what a tire gauge reads); absolute pressure adds $P_0$. Pressure depends only on depth, not on the container's shape.

Pascal's principle: a pressure change is transmitted undiminished through an enclosed fluid, so a hydraulic lift multiplies force: $F_2 = F_1 A_2/A_1$ (but the small piston moves farther: work is conserved).

Archimedes: the buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid, $F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}} V_{\text{sub}}\, g$. A floating object has $F_B = mg$, so the submerged fraction is $\rho_{\text{obj}}/\rho_{\text{fluid}}$. A fully submerged object sinks if $\rho_{\text{obj}} > \rho_{\text{fluid}}$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 10.1–10.3
SECTIONS.title: Rotational kinematics
ideas: Angle $\theta$ in radians, angular velocity $\omega = d\theta/dt$ (rad/s), angular acceleration $\alpha = d\omega/dt$ (rad/s²). One revolution is $2\pi$ rad; rpm converts by $\omega = \text{rpm}\times 2\pi/60$.
Constant $\alpha$ obeys the same four equations as 1D kinematics with $x\to\theta$, $v\to\omega$, $a\to\alpha$.

Link to a point at radius $r$: arc length $s = r\theta$, tangential speed $v = r\omega$, tangential acceleration $a_t = r\alpha$, centripetal acceleration $a_c = r\omega^2$. Total acceleration magnitude $\sqrt{a_t^2 + a_c^2}$.
Every point on a rigid body shares the same $\omega$ and $\alpha$; points farther out move faster.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 7
SECTIONS.title: Work, kinetic energy, and power
ideas: Work by a constant force: $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d = Fd\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is between the force and the displacement. Forces perpendicular to motion (normal force, centripetal tension) do zero work; friction on a sliding object does negative work.
Variable force: $W = \int F_x\,dx$ = area under the $F$–$x$ graph. A spring stretched from 0 to $x$ stores $\tfrac12 kx^2$.
Work–energy theorem: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \tfrac12 mv_f^2 - \tfrac12 mv_i^2$. It replaces kinematics when you know forces and distances but do not care about time.
Power is the rate of doing work: $P = W/t = \vec F\cdot\vec v$. Units: watt; $1\ \text{hp} = 746$ W. Lifting at constant speed: $P = mgv$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 8
SECTIONS.title: Potential energy and conservation of energy
ideas: Conservative forces (gravity, springs) have potential energy: $U_g = mgy$ (any zero level you like), $U_s = \tfrac12 kx^2$. Their work is path-independent and $W_c = -\Delta U$.

Conservation of mechanical energy when only conservative forces do work: $K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$. With friction or other non-conservative forces: $K_i + U_i + W_{nc} = K_f + U_f$, where $W_{nc} = -f_k d$ for kinetic friction.
Speed at the bottom of a frictionless track depends only on the height drop, not on the path: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
Energy diagrams: the object moves where $E \ge U(x)$; turning points are where $E = U$; equilibrium where $dU/dx = 0$ (stable at a minimum of $U$).
Energy is a scalar: no components, no directions. That is why it is often the easiest tool.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 9.1–9.3
SECTIONS.title: Momentum and impulse
ideas: Momentum $\vec p = m\vec v$ is a vector. Newton's second law in its general form: $\sum\vec F = d\vec p/dt$.

Impulse–momentum theorem: $\vec J = \int\vec F\,dt = \vec F_{\text{avg}}\Delta t = \Delta\vec p$. A longer collision time means a smaller average force for the same momentum change (airbags, bending your knees).

Conservation of momentum: if the net external force on a system is zero (or the collision is so brief that external impulses are negligible), total momentum is conserved: $\sum\vec p_i = \sum\vec p_f$, component by component.
Recoil: a gun and bullet start at rest, so $m_g v_g = -m_b v_b$. Explosions and rockets work the same way.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 9.4–9.6
SECTIONS.title: Collisions and center of mass
ideas: All collisions in an isolated system conserve momentum. Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy; inelastic ones lose some KE (to heat, sound, deformation); perfectly inelastic ones stick together and lose the most KE possible.

Perfectly inelastic: $v_f = \dfrac{m_1v_1 + m_2v_2}{m_1+m_2}$. Elastic with target at rest: $v_{1f} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1+m_2}v_{1i}$, $v_{2f} = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}v_{1i}$. Equal masses swap velocities.
2D collisions: conserve $p_x$ and $p_y$ separately. Draw before and after pictures with angles.

Center of mass $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i}$ moves as if all mass were there and all external forces acted on it. Internal forces (explosions, collisions) never change the center-of-mass motion.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 10.4–10.8
SECTIONS.title: Rotational dynamics
ideas: Moment of inertia $I = \sum m_ir_i^2$ (or $\int r^2\,dm$) is rotational mass: it depends on how far the mass sits from the axis. Point mass $mr^2$; hoop $MR^2$; solid disk/cylinder $\tfrac12 MR^2$; solid sphere $\tfrac25 MR^2$; thin rod about center $\tfrac1{12}ML^2$, about end $\tfrac13 ML^2$.
Newton's second law for rotation: $\sum\tau = I\alpha$ about a fixed axis. Torque from a force at radius $r$: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$.
Rotational kinetic energy $K = \tfrac12 I\omega^2$. Work by a torque $W = \tau\theta$; power $P = \tau\omega$. The work–energy theorem holds with these.
Parallel-axis theorem: $I = I_{cm} + Md^2$.
Pulley with mass: the two rope tensions differ, and $(T_1 - T_2)R = I\alpha$ with $a = R\alpha$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 11
SECTIONS.title: Rolling motion and angular momentum
ideas: Rolling without slipping: $v_{cm} = R\omega$, $a_{cm} = R\alpha$. Total KE $= \tfrac12 mv_{cm}^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2$. Rolling down a ramp: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1 + I/(mR^2)}}$, so a sphere ($\tfrac25$) beats a disk ($\tfrac12$) beats a hoop ($1$), independent of mass and radius.
Angular momentum of a rigid body $L = I\omega$; of a particle $L = mvr\sin\theta$ ($= mvr$ for circular motion). Newton for rotation: $\sum\vec\tau = d\vec L/dt$.
Conservation: with zero net external torque, $L$ is conserved. Ice skater pulling in arms: $I$ drops so $\omega$ rises ($I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f$); kinetic energy increases (the skater does work).
Direction by the right-hand rule: curl fingers with the rotation, thumb gives $\vec\omega$ and $\vec L$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 13
SECTIONS.title: Gravitation
ideas: Newton's law of gravitation: $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$, attractive, along the line joining the centers, with $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. $r$ is measured from center to center.
Surface gravity $g = GM/R^2$ (Earth: $M = 5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, $R = 6.37\times10^6$ m gives 9.8). At altitude $h$: $g = g_0\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^2$.
Circular orbits: gravity supplies the centripetal force, $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}$ (Kepler's third law). Faster orbits are lower.

Gravitational potential energy with the zero at infinity: $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. Orbital energy $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ (negative: bound). Escape speed from a surface: $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ (11.2 km/s for Earth).
Kepler: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus; equal areas in equal times (angular momentum conservation); $T^2 \propto a^3$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 15.1–15.3
SECTIONS.title: Simple harmonic motion
ideas: SHM happens whenever the restoring force is proportional to displacement: $F = -kx$ gives $a = -\dfrac{k}{m}x$. Solution $x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ with $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$, period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, frequency $f = 1/T$.

Velocity $v(t) = -A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi)$, acceleration $a(t) = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t+\phi) = -\omega^2 x$. Max speed $A\omega$ at the center; max acceleration $A\omega^2$ at the extremes (where $v = 0$).
The period does not depend on amplitude (for an ideal spring) or on $g$ (a vertical spring just shifts the equilibrium point).
Energy: $E = \tfrac12 kA^2 = \tfrac12 mv^2 + \tfrac12 kx^2$, sloshing between kinetic and potential. Speed at position $x$: $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$.
SHM is the shadow of uniform circular motion: the projection of a point moving on a circle of radius $A$ at angular speed $\omega$.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 15.4–15.6
SECTIONS.title: Pendulums, damping, and resonance
ideas: Simple pendulum (small angles): $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, independent of mass and (for small swings) amplitude. Physical pendulum: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgd)}$ with $d$ from pivot to center of mass.
Measuring $g$: time many swings, $g = 4\pi^2L/T^2$. Longer pendulum, longer period; on the Moon the period grows.
Damping: friction or drag makes the amplitude decay exponentially; the frequency drops slightly. Underdamped oscillates, critically damped returns fastest without oscillating, overdamped creeps back.

Forced oscillations and resonance: driving at the natural frequency $\omega_0$ produces the largest amplitude (pushing a swing, shattering glass, Tacoma Narrows). Less damping makes the resonance peak sharper and taller.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 16
SECTIONS.title: Mechanical waves
ideas: A wave carries energy, not matter. Transverse (string) vs longitudinal (sound). Wavelength $\lambda$, period $T$, frequency $f = 1/T$, speed $v = \lambda f = \lambda/T$. The speed is set by the medium; the frequency by the source.
Wave function $y(x,t) = A\sin(kx - \omega t + \phi)$ with wave number $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ and $\omega = 2\pi f$; speed $v = \omega/k$. The minus sign means motion in $+x$.
String: $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$ ($\mu$ = mass per length). Tighter or lighter strings carry faster waves. Wave power $\propto A^2 f^2$.
Superposition: waves add. In phase → constructive; half a wavelength out of phase → destructive. Reflection from a fixed end inverts the pulse.
Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends: $\lambda_n = 2L/n$, $f_n = n\dfrac{v}{2L}$ ($n = 1,2,3,\dots$). Nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart; the fundamental has one antinode.

SECTIONS.label: Ch 17
SECTIONS.title: Sound
ideas: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave. Speed in air about 343 m/s at 20 °C (rises with temperature); much faster in water and solids. $v = f\lambda$ still.

Intensity $I = P/A$ (W/m²) falls off as $1/r^2$ from a point source. Sound level in decibels: $\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ with $I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2$. Every $+10$ dB is $\times10$ intensity; $+3$ dB is about $\times2$.
Pipes: open–open resonates at $f_n = n\dfrac{v}{2L}$ (all harmonics); closed–open at $f_n = n\dfrac{v}{4L}$ with odd $n$ only.
Beats: two close frequencies produce a loudness wobble at $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2|$.
Doppler effect: $f' = f\dfrac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$. Top signs for approach (observer toward source: $+v_o$; source toward observer: $-v_s$). Approaching raises pitch.
